newsitem.title: JAPAN: Western investors shy away from Japan real estate.
newsitem.headline: Western investors shy away from Japan real estate.

text.p: Western investors are shunning Japanese real estate despite a recent, high-profile move by an Asian investor to snap up a prime Tokyo site, experts say.
They say the lack of liquidity and other factors peculiar to Japan's property market were keeping them away.

"Fund managers from the U.S. and Europe have started coming to us recently to talk about Japan's real estate market, but once we tell them the facts, they back off," said Yukio Furuta, investment director at Richard Ellis, an international property consultant firm.
Furuta said one of the biggest turnoffs for Western investors was Japan's national land use planning law, which virtually controls land prices and hinders liquidity in the property market.

The law, for instance, requires Japan's Land Agency to be informed in advance of transactions of land more than 2,000 square metres (2,390 sq yards), which then checks to see if the prices were properly set.
"This kind of rule is not seen in other industrialised nations," Furuta said. As a result, premium property rarely changes hands in Japan, he said.

Recent auctions of land belonging to the former Japan National Railways gave foreigners a rare chance to bid for prime Japanese real estate, and the high prices they attracted raised hopes that Japan's property market has bottomed out.

In one, a Japanese unit of Pacific Century Group bought land near the Tokyo railway station for 86.8 billion yen ($717 million), far higher than analysts' forecasts of about 45 billion yen ($371 million).
Pacific Century Group is headed by Hong Kong-born businessman Richard Li, son of Li Ka-shing, one of the richest men in the world.
Commercial land prices in Tokyo have fallen more than 80 percent from their peak in 1991 after the bursting of the "bubble economy" of inflated asset prices.

Hiroshi Yamamura, director of economic research at NLI Research Institute, said overall commercial land prices were still high compared to other countries and may need to fall by about 50 percent or more to become attractive to investors.
It is not known yet if the government's announcement earlier this week that it was drawing up measures to improve land liquidity would have any impact on the market, analysts said.

Furuta said the market needed more than Asian investors to perk it up. "Asian money alone cannot improve the property market. Western investors, and Japanese individuals who hold 1,200 trillion yen ($9.75 trillion) in savings, are also needed."
He also doubted that the purchases by Asian investors were purely for long-term investments, because they generally prefer to seek short-term profits.
Japanese property owners tend to look for stable income growth through renting office space for the long term, while Western investors tend to seek capital gains through transactions, Furuta added.
European and American investors put greater emphasis on the idea of "cash flow-based value" on real estate, Furuta said.

Building owners in Japan must pay various maintenance costs, including taxes and insurance, making it difficult for Western investors to gauge net earnings when they invest here. In Brtiain, tenants shoulder those costs, Furuta said. ($1=123 yen)
